chunks: "The big picture is that surface-mount wins on density, automation and high-frequency behaviour, and through-hole wins on mechanical strength and power handling.
With surface-mount, parts sit on pads and a pick-and-place machine puts them down and a reflow oven solders them all at once, both sides of the board if needed.
The parts are smaller, so the board shrinks, and the leads are short, so inductance is lower, which matters for decoupling and high-speed signals.
Through-hole parts have leads that go through plated holes.
They're bigger and need drilling, which uses board space on every layer, and assembly is by wave or selective soldering or by hand, so it's slower and costs more in volume.

A connector that gets plugged in a thousand times, a big electrolytic capacitor, a transformer, or a TO-220 bolted to a heat sink gets its mechanical strength from the leads and barrel, not from a small solder fillet.
Through-hole is also easier to prototype, because you can hand-solder it and use it on a breadboard.
In practice most boards are mixed: SMT for the bulk of the parts, through-hole for connectors and heavy or high-power parts, sometimes with through-hole tabs on SMD connectors for strength.
I'd pick based on size, frequency, mechanical load and who will assemble it."
